Unit 1 of 10: Scarcity, Choice and Opportunity Cost

Key ideas

  • Scarcity: human wants are unlimited, but resources are limited. This forces choices.
  • The factors of production:
  • land (natural resources), which earns rent;
  • labour, which earns wages;
  • capital (man-made aids to production), which earns interest;
  • entrepreneurship, which earns profit.
  • Opportunity cost: the value of the next best alternative that is given up.
  • Free goods have no opportunity cost; economic goods do.
  • The production possibilities curve (PPC):
  • it shows the maximum combinations of two goods that can be produced with all resources fully and efficiently used;
  • a point inside the curve shows unemployment or inefficiency;
  • a point outside the curve is unattainable;
  • an outward shift shows economic growth;
  • the curve bows outwards because of increasing opportunity cost: resources are not equally suited to producing both goods.
  • The basic economic questions: what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom.
  • Economic systems: the free market, planned and mixed economies.

Worked examples

Example 1: a government spends ₹1 000 crore on a new metro line instead of hospitals. The opportunity cost is the hospitals that are not built.

Example 2: a move from point B (inside) to point A (on the PPC) uses resources that were unemployed. Output rises with no opportunity cost.

Example 3: better education raises the quality of labour, which shifts the PPC outwards.

10-mark exam-style question

Using a production possibilities curve diagram, explain how an economy can achieve economic growth. [10]

Markband guidance (our version):

  • 9–10 marks:
  • accurate definitions of economic growth and the PPC;
  • a correctly labelled diagram showing both a movement from inside to the curve (actual growth) and an outward shift (potential growth);
  • an explanation of the causes, such as more or better factors of production and technology;
  • effective, relevant real-world examples.
  • 5–8 marks: some of the above, with less development.
  • 1–4 marks: limited understanding, or no diagram.

Common mistakes

  1. Leaving the axes unlabelled.
  2. Confusing a movement along the PPC with a shift.
  3. Defining opportunity cost as "the cost of something".
  4. Leaving out the reason for the curve's bowed shape.
  5. Giving no real-world example.

Quick recall

  1. What is opportunity cost?
  2. What does a point inside the PPC show?
  3. Name the four factors of production.
  4. Why is the PPC bowed outwards?
  5. What causes the PPC to shift outwards?

Answers: 1) The next best alternative forgone. 2) Unemployment or inefficiency. 3) Land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. 4) Increasing opportunity cost. 5) More or better resources, or improved technology.
